claims.statement: Troubleshooting article applies to FPT/GHEC, not GHES. Custom Actions publishing ignores repository CNAME files and does not require them; subsequent CNAME existence/format instructions apply to branch publication, not universally.

Branch custom-domain storage is uppercase CNAME at publishing-source root, editable through settings or manually. Management guide describes settings-generated commit at source-branch root; preserve location wording distinction for folder sources rather than certify every root layout.

Locally generated or force-pushed branch output can overwrite the settings-created CNAME; source recommends incorporating that commit into local output first. This warning does not authorize force pushes or prove safe synchronization.

Branch CNAME contains one domain name only and must be unique across Pages sites. Multiple external names require provider redirects; file syntax or uniqueness claims are not proof of owned-domain association.

DNS-provider support, dig or an online DNS lookup can diagnose records. DNS answers alone do not establish effective Pages configuration, permission, ownership verification, certificate validity or reader restrictions.

Unsupported combinations include more than one apex, more than one www subdomain, or apex together with a non-www custom subdomain. Paired www/apex is an exception; article describes www-to-apex direction, while management guide allows direction toward whichever custom domain is selected.
Wildcard DNS remains takeover-exposed even after domain verification, including deeper descendants outside immediate-subdomain protection. Do not treat verification as recursive wildcard assurance.

Correct CNAME, ALIAS, ANAME or A DNS configurations support HTTPS according to source. AAAA is absent from this list despite management IPv6 examples; absence is not proof that IPv6 is categorically unsupported.

Source says HTTPS can become available up to one hour after configuration, while management includes up to 24 hours for Enforce HTTPS option availability and DNS propagation. These measure different conditions and are not actual runtime receipts.

After existing DNS changes the guide suggests possibly removing and re-adding the repository domain to retrigger HTTPS provisioning. This mutates native association and can disrupt service; it requires exact approval and recovery planning, not automatic diagnostic execution.

Where CAA records are used, source requires at least one letsencrypt.org value for HTTPS. This historical shorthand is not a complete audited CAA record schema, current CA policy or authority to change DNS.

Source claims Linux browsing server errors for account names beginning/ending in dash or containing consecutive dashes and suggests username change. This platform-specific claim remains unverified; account rename has broader identity/URL effects and is not authorized here.

Browser cache clearing is a possible diagnostic after domain changes, not proof the authoritative DNS/site state is correct. Domain-already-used guidance suggests verification, qualified by verification guide: already verified elsewhere cannot simply be reclaimed.

All procedures and linked references remain pinned-source evidence, not accepted policy, exhaustive published assurance, legal clearance or native recovery results. No source commands, DNS changes, account renames or domain reassociations were executed.
